reasons: The clause does grant our side a no-cause termination right: ¶4(a) says 'Either Party may terminate this Agreement for any reason following the Initial Term upon ninety (90) days written notice,' and p0000 defines Customer as a 'Party.' The failed deterministic check is a string-matching artifact (the operative sentence uses 'Either Party' rather than 'Customer'), not a substantive gap.

Material fallback terms are met: Customer convenience notice of 90 days sits at the top of the 60–90 day fallback band; the term is a 1-year Initial Term with 1-year auto-renewals, so the walk-away trigger ('no Customer right to terminate for convenience in a multi-year term') is not engaged; and Vendor's convenience notice is 90 days, i.e. not 'fewer than 90 days.'

The Kubient entitlement to 'all fees generated during the termination period' is at worst equivalent to fees over the 90-day notice window, which is within the fallback's 3-months'-fees cap, so it is not a disqualifying exit penalty.

The two shortfalls identified (90 days rather than the preferred 30, and no pro-rata prepaid-fee refund) are minor sub-elements properly noted in the rationale rather than escalated; the refund point is genuinely moot under the §5 revenue-share/sequential-liability model where nothing is prepaid.

Vendor's ability to exit mid-renewal rather than strictly at term end is the weakest point against the fallback, but it is exactly reciprocal to our own right on identical notice within a 1-year renewal cycle, so it benefits us equally and does not warrant a redline under the 'do not flag a clause that benefits our party' guidance.
Presentation matches a compliant finding: no redline text was altered and no counterparty comment was emitted, which is correct for a clause sitting at the fallback.
